passages.happening:
Paul and Silas pass through Amphipolis and Apollonia and come to Thessalonica, where there is a Jewish synagogue (verse 1). As is his custom, Paul goes in, and on three Sabbaths he reasons with them from the Scriptures (verse 2), “explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead” (verse 3). “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ,” he says.

Some of the Jews are persuaded and join Paul and Silas, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Amphipolis and Apollonia were towns on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road across Macedonia. Thessalonica, today's Thessaloniki, was the chief city of the province, a Greek city that ran its own affairs.

‘As was his custom.’ Even after being beaten in Philippi, Paul goes first to the synagogue. The good news is about Israel's Messiah, and he brings it to Israel first.

‘Reasoned’, ‘explaining’, ‘proving’: these are words of argument and discussion, not of shouting. Over three Sabbaths Paul opens the Scriptures with his hearers and argues from them.

His hardest point is that ‘the Christ had to suffer’. ‘Christ’ is the Greek form of ‘Messiah’, the anointed King God had promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would win, not one who would be crucified; Paul later wrote that a crucified Christ was ‘a stumbling block to Jews’ (1 Corinthians 1:23). Paul has to show from their own Bible that suffering was part of God's plan for his King, and that the King would rise.

The response is mixed, as it will be in town after town. Some Jews believe. So do many ‘God-fearing Greeks’, Gentiles who already worshipped Israel's God, and ‘quite a few leading women’, women of the city's important families.
passages.ot:
Which Scriptures did Paul use? Luke does not list them here, but the early church often turned to Isaiah's servant: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). After his resurrection Jesus himself asked, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26), and opened the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms to show it.

And the Psalms promised that God would raise up his King: “I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6).
passages.asks: Paul reasoned, explained and gave evidence, week after week. Ask whether you can explain from the Bible why Jesus had to suffer, or whether you only know that he did. And ask whether you are willing to talk and listen patiently, the way Paul did, rather than simply to announce.

passages.happening:
“The Jews, however, became jealous” (verse 5). They gather some troublemakers from the marketplace, form a mob, and set the city in an uproar. They raid the house of Jason, looking for Paul and Silas.

When they cannot find them, they drag Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here” (verse 6), and Jason has taken them in. “They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus” (verse 7).

The crowd and the officials are greatly disturbed (verse 8). The officials take a bond, a sum of money as security, from Jason and the others, and let them go (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Who does Luke mean by ‘the Jews’ here? Not the Jewish people, and not even all the Jews of Thessalonica, since some of them had just believed (verse 4). He means some of the synagogue's members and leaders in this city, who opposed Paul. Paul and Silas, who are being hunted, are Jews too. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Jason was a believer who had welcomed Paul and Silas into his home. He pays for it. He is dragged before the court and has to put up money as a pledge that there will be no more trouble.

The ‘city officials’ are called in Greek politarchs, ‘rulers of the city’. Luke's title is a rare one, and inscriptions using it have been found in Thessalonica; the best known came from an old arch over the main Roman road and is now in the British Museum.

Now the charge. ‘Turned the world upside down’ means troublemakers who unsettle every place they go. And they say ‘there is another king, named Jesus’. In a Roman city that was a charge of disloyalty to the emperor, the most dangerous charge there was. It twisted what Paul taught. He did proclaim Jesus as King, the Messiah, but not as a rebel leader raising an army against Rome. Jesus himself had said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

This scene has sometimes been pulled into modern political arguments of one kind or another. These notes make no such use of it. Luke is telling how a mob twisted the message in one city, in the first century.
passages.ot:
The charge was false, but the claim behind it was true: Jesus is the King the Scriptures promised. Zechariah saw him coming in a strange way, “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). This King did not seize his throne by force.

The Old Testament also knows faithful people accused of disloyalty to a foreign king. Daniel's enemies said they would never find a charge against him “unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God” (Daniel 6:5).
passages.asks: The believers were called people who turn the world upside down. Ask whether anyone would notice a difference if your faith reached your town. And notice the twist: a message about a humble King was told as a plot against the state. Ask how carefully you represent other people's beliefs, especially beliefs you oppose.

passages.t: Berea: searching the Scriptures every day
passages.happening:
As soon as night falls, the believers send Paul and Silas away to Berea. There they go into the Jewish synagogue (verse 10). “Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (verse 11). Many of them believe, along with quite a few prominent Greek women and men (verse 12).

But when some from Thessalonica hear that Paul is preaching in Berea, they come and stir up the crowds there too (verse 13). The believers send Paul off to the coast at once, while Silas and Timothy stay in Berea (verse 14). His escorts bring him to Athens, and go back with word for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as they can (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Berea is today's Veria, a town to the west of Thessalonica.

Luke praises the Jews of Berea, and the reason matters. They were ‘noble-minded’, which means open and generous in mind. They listened eagerly. And then they checked. Every day they ‘examined the Scriptures’ to see if what Paul said was true. They did not swallow the message whole, and they did not reject it unheard. They tested an apostle's words against the Bible, and Luke counts that as noble.

The Scriptures they searched were what Christians now call the Old Testament. The New Testament had not yet been written. Paul was showing them that their own Bible pointed to Jesus.

Verse 13 says ‘the Jews from Thessalonica’. Luke means the same opponents from Thessalonica as before, who travel to Berea to stir up trouble, not the Jews of Berea, many of whom have just believed. The note on verses 5-9 above says more about how to read Luke's ‘the Jews’.
passages.ot:
The Bereans did what the Law asked of Israel, to weigh a prophet's words: if a prophet speaks in the LORD's name and his word does not come true, “the prophet has spoken presumptuously” (Deuteronomy 18:22). And the Psalms commend the one whose delight is in the LORD's law, who meditates on it “day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

God had promised that those who seek him will find him: “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). The Bereans searched, and many found.
passages.asks: The Bereans listened eagerly and then checked everything against the Scriptures. Ask whether you do either. Some people believe whatever a favourite teacher says; others dismiss what they have not heard out. Test what you hear, including these notes, against the Bible itself.

passages.t: Athens: a city full of idols
passages.happening:
While Paul waits in Athens, he is “deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols” (verse 16). So he reasons in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace every day with whoever is there (verse 17).

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers begin to debate with him. Some ask, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others say, “He seems to be advocating foreign gods”, because Paul is proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection (verse 18).

So they bring him to the Areopagus and ask, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?” (verse 19). They want to know what these strange ideas mean (verse 20). Luke adds that all the Athenians and the foreigners living there spend their time doing nothing more than hearing and talking about new ideas (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Athens had long lost its power, but it was still famous for its learning and its schools of philosophy. A Roman city was crowded with gods: temples in the main square, altars at the crossroads, statues of gods and emperors on every side. Paul, a Jew who knew the commandment against images, walks through it and is ‘deeply disturbed’.

He does two things at once. On the Sabbath he speaks in the synagogue. On other days he goes to the marketplace, the agora, the open square where people bought and sold, met and argued, and he talks with anyone who will listen.

There he meets two kinds of philosopher. The Stoics took their name from the stoa, a public porch in Athens where their founder, Zeno, taught. They believed that a divine reason runs through the whole world and orders it, and that goodness of character is the only thing truly worth having.

The Epicureans followed Epicurus, who lived from about 341 to 271 BC. He taught that the gods, if they exist, are far away and take no part in human life, and that the soul is made of fine particles that scatter at death. The good life, for him, was a simple, quiet pleasure, free from pain and fear.

Neither group expected a dead man to rise. Some call Paul a ‘babbler’, in Greek a ‘seed-picker’, a bird that pecks up scraps, used of a man who picks up scraps of ideas. Others think he is preaching ‘foreign gods’, perhaps because he speaks of ‘Jesus and the resurrection’. Some readers think they heard the Greek word for resurrection, anastasis, as the name of a second god.

They bring him to the Areopagus. The name means ‘hill of Ares’, a hill near the Acropolis, and it was also the name of the city's ancient council, which had once met there. By Paul's day the council may have met in the marketplace, and scholars differ on whether Paul spoke on the hill itself or before the council elsewhere. Either way, it was a hearing to find out what he taught, not necessarily a trial.
passages.ot:
Paul's distress at idols comes straight from the Law and the Prophets. The first commandments forbid other gods and carved images (Exodus 20:3-4). Isaiah mocked the making of idols: “All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless” (Isaiah 44:9). “To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?” (Isaiah 40:18).

And the resurrection Paul preached was the hope of the prophets: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.asks: Paul was deeply troubled by what his city worshipped, and his trouble sent him to talk with people, not away from them. Ask what your town worships: its idols may be money, success, comfort or image rather than statues. And ask whether what troubles you sends you toward people or away from them.

passages.happening:
Paul stands up in the meeting of the Areopagus and says, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious” (verse 22). As he walked around, he found an altar with the inscription, TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. “Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you” (verse 23).

“The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands” (verse 24). He is not served by human hands as if he needed anything, “because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else” (verse 25).

“From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth” (verse 26), and he set their times and the boundaries of their lands. God meant them to seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, “though He is not far from each one of us” (verse 27). “For in Him we live and move and have our being.” As some of their own poets have said, “We are His offspring” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
This speech shows how Paul speaks to people who have no Bible. In the synagogue he began with Israel's story and the prophets. Here he begins with what his hearers already see: their own altars, their own poets, the world around them. Every claim he makes comes from the Scriptures, but he does not quote chapter and verse to people who have never read them.

He starts politely: ‘very religious’. The Greek word can mean devout or it can mean superstitious, and Paul may mean a little of both.

Then the altar. Ancient writers mention altars at Athens to ‘unknown gods’. The travel writer Pausanias, in the second century AD, speaks of them, and a later writer, Diogenes Laertius, tells a story of altars set up without a god's name in a time of plague, so that no god would be left out. No altar with the exact words Paul quotes has been found. Paul takes the inscription as his starting point. You admit there is a God you do not know. I have come to tell you who he is.

Then he says plainly who God is. He made everything. He does not live in temples, however beautiful; the Parthenon stood on the Acropolis nearby. He needs nothing from us; we need everything from him. He made all nations from one man, so no nation, not even proud Athens, is better born than the rest. And he is near. People were made to seek him.

Then two quotations. ‘We are His offspring’ comes from a poem by Aratus, a Greek poet from Cilicia, Paul's own region, who lived in the third century BC; his poem Phaenomena opens with praise of Zeus, and a Stoic hymn by Cleanthes uses similar words. ‘In Him we live and move and have our being’ is often traced to the Cretan poet Epimenides, but that is less certain, and some think it was simply a common Greek saying. Aratus wrote his line about Zeus. Paul takes the words and gives them a fuller meaning: the true God, the Maker, is the one in whom we live.
passages.ot:
Paul does not quote the Old Testament here, but every line rests on it. God made the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1), and “gives breath to the people on it and life to those who walk in it” (Isaiah 42:5). Solomon prayed at the temple he had built, “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27). God needs nothing: “the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 50:12).

All people come from one: God made man in his own image (Genesis 1:27), and “When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance” he “set the boundaries of the peoples” (Deuteronomy 32:8). And the call to seek him is the Law's own promise: “you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 4:29).
passages.hard:
How should Christians speak to people who do not share their Bible? Paul at Athens has been read in more than one way.

Some readers note that Paul began from common ground: an altar, a poet, creation itself. They see a model here for speaking to people today who do not know the Bible: start where people are, take their questions and their best thinkers seriously, and show where their own longings point. Paul later wrote that God's power and nature “have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship” (Romans 1:20).

Others are more cautious. They note that Paul does not leave the Athenians where they are. He tells them God has overlooked their ignorance but now commands them to repent, and he names the resurrection, which he knew they would find absurd. The common ground is a door, not a place to stay.

Most readers hold both: Paul met his hearers with courtesy and real knowledge of their world, and he did not trim the message to fit it.
passages.asks: Paul knew the Athenians' altars and quoted their poets. He had paid attention to their world. Ask whether you know the hopes, questions and favourite voices of the people around you well enough to begin where they are. And take his central claim personally: God ‘is not far from each one of us’. That includes you.

passages.t: ‘He has set a day’: some mock, some believe
passages.happening:
“Therefore, being offspring of God, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination” (verse 29). God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, but “He now commands all people everywhere to repent” (verse 30). “For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead” (verse 31).

When they hear about the resurrection of the dead, some begin to mock. Others say, “We want to hear you again on this topic” (verse 32). So Paul leaves the Areopagus (verse 33). But some join him and believe, among them Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others with them (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Paul turns his hearers' poet against their idols. If we are God's offspring, living people, then God cannot be like a lump of gold or stone that we have shaped. The maker cannot be smaller than what he made.

Then the turn. God has been patient with ‘the ignorance of earlier times’. But now he ‘commands all people everywhere to repent’. To repent means to turn around: to change one's mind and the direction of one's life. For these hearers it meant turning from idols to the living God.

Why now? Because God has fixed a day of judgment, and he has named the judge: ‘the Man He has appointed’. And he has given proof: he raised that man from the dead.

That is where the Athenians stop listening. Neither the Stoics nor the Epicureans looked for a dead body to rise, and to many Greeks the idea was foolish. Paul later wrote that the message of the cross is ‘foolishness to Gentiles’ (1 Corinthians 1:23). The resurrection is the sticking point. Paul could have stopped before it and kept his audience. He did not.

The results are mixed. Some mock. Some want to hear more. And some believe. Luke names two. Dionysius was a member of the council itself, a man of high standing. Damaris was a woman; Luke tells us nothing more about her, but he wanted her name remembered. Paul did not plant a large church in Athens, as far as Acts tells, but he did not leave empty-handed.
passages.ot:
The argument against idols is the prophets' argument. Isaiah asked, “Who fashions a god or casts an idol which profits him nothing?” (Isaiah 44:10), and Psalm 115 says idols have mouths but cannot speak.

The coming judgment is the hope of the Psalms: “He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness” (Psalm 96:13). And Daniel saw “one like the Son of Man” given authority over all nations (Daniel 7:13-14), the judge Paul now names.
passages.hard:
Did Paul's approach at Athens fail? Some readers point out that few believed in Athens, and that when Paul went on to Corinth he wrote that he had resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). They think Paul learned from Athens to drop philosophical argument.

Others see no such regret. Luke presents the speech as a model, not a failure: some did believe, including a member of the council, and what Paul says matches his letters (compare Romans 1:18-25). On this reading Paul's words to the Corinthians are about the showy speech that Corinth admired, not about meeting people where they are.

Both readings agree on one thing. Paul did not water down the resurrection, even when it brought mockery.
passages.asks: Paul could have stopped before the resurrection and kept the Athenians smiling. He named it, and some laughed. Ask whether you leave out the parts of the faith your friends find hardest to accept. And remember Damaris and Dionysius: when the crowd mocks, someone may still be listening.
